stdout_tail:
Analysis complete. With default hyperparameters and identical preprocessing/CV folds, logistic regression (mean ROC-AUC 0.9067) slightly **outperformed** the default random forest (0.9023) on this dataset — a difference of -0.0043 (RF - LogReg), consistent across all 5 folds. This makes sense: `RandomForestClassifier()` defaults to unlimited-depth trees (no `max_depth`), which tends to overfit on tabular data like this without tuning, while default `LogisticRegression()` benefits from the largely linear/monotonic relationships between features like education, hours-worked, and capital-gain and the income target.

Results saved to `result.json`, code saved to `analysis.py`.

parsed_result.summary: Using stratified 5-fold CV, RandomForestClassifier() achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.9023 versus 0.9067 for LogisticRegression(), a difference of -0.0043, so the random forest does not outperform logistic regression on this dataset with default hyperparameters.
parsed_result.methodological_choices: Target encoded as class=='>50K' -> 1. Missing values in categorical columns (workclass, occupation, native-country; originally '?' in raw data) imputed with an explicit 'Missing' category rather than dropping rows; numeric missing values (none present) would be median-imputed. Categorical features one-hot encoded (handle_unknown='ignore'); numeric features standard-scaled. The identical preprocessing pipeline and identical StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) splits were used for both models to make the comparison paired and fair, even though scaling is not required for RandomForest. No class-imbalance handling applied (roughly 24%/76% class split; ROC-AUC is relatively robust to this imbalance). Both classifiers use pure scikit-learn defaults (RandomForestClassifier(), LogisticRegression()) with only random_state set for reproducibility of the RF and of the CV splitter itself, not as a hyperparameter choice. Metric: mean ROC-AUC across the 5 folds.
